changes.new: ### A complete accumulated step and two incorrect orders For a scalar parameter $\theta$, let two microbatches contain two and six tokens. Give every token in the first microbatch the loss $2\theta$, and every token in the second the loss $10\theta$. The mean loss over all eight tokens is $8\theta$, so its gradient is 8. The two microbatches contribute $2\cdot2/8=0.5$ and $6\cdot10/8=7.5$. With a fixed loss scale $S=128$, the first backward pass writes 64 to the gradient buffer. The second adds 960. The accumulated buffer is 1024; one division by 128 recovers 8. Neither backward pass should clear the buffer. The division by eight in each loss supplies token weighting; the multiplication by 128 supplies loss scaling. These are separate operations. | Point in the step | Gradient buffer | |---|---:| | After the first scaled backward | 64 | | After the second scaled backward | 1024 | | After one unscale | 8 | | Parameter after SGD with learning rate 0.25, starting at 1 | -1 | PyTorch's [gradient accumulation instructions](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/notes/amp_examples.html#gradient-accumulation) state: > Also, grads should remain scaled, and the scale factor should remain constant, while grads for a given effective batch are accumulated. The following example uses the actual CPU `GradScaler` API and autograd. It deliberately uses FP32 scalar arithmetic without `autocast`: its purpose is to verify accumulation and optimizer ordering, not FP16 underflow or CUDA execution. ~~~python import torch theta = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.tensor(1.0)) optimizer = torch.optim.SGD([theta], lr=0.25) scaler = torch.amp.GradScaler("cpu", init_scale=128.0) optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True) for count, slope in [(2, 2.0), (6, 10.0)]: token_slopes = torch.full((count,), slope) loss = (theta * token_slopes).sum() / 8 scaler.scale(loss).backward() assert theta.grad.item() == 1024.0 scaler.unscale_(optimizer) assert theta.grad.item() == 8.0 scaler.step(optimizer) scaler.update() assert theta.item() == -1.0 print(theta.grad.item(), theta.item()) # 8.0 -1.0 ~~~ Unscaling after only the first microbatch changes 64 into 0.5. A subsequent scaled backward then adds 960, leaving 960.5. The buffer now mixes units. Calling `unscale_` a second time is not a repair: this API rejects a second unscale of the same optimizer before the next update. Calling `step` without that second call is also wrong. The scaler remembers the earlier unscale and does not divide again; ordinary SGD would use 960.5 as the gradient. Changing scales between microbatches causes a different mixture. Scaling the first contribution by 128 and the second by 64 gives $64+480=544$. Dividing by 64 gives 8.5, while dividing by 128 gives 4.25. A common final division cannot restore the desired sum 8 from these differently scaled contributions. ### Clipping before unscale changes the threshold Consider an unscaled two-parameter gradient $g=(3,4)$, whose norm is 5. For a norm threshold of 1, ideal norm clipping gives $g_{\mathrm{clip}}=(0.6,0.8)$. With $S=8$, the scaled gradient is $(24,32)$, with norm 40. Clipping that vector to norm 1 also produces $(0.6,0.8)$, but a subsequent division by eight shrinks it to $(0.075,0.1)$, with norm 0.125. The intended threshold of 1 has become $1/S$ in unscaled units. For nonzero $g$, positive $S$ and a nonnegative threshold $c$, the two orders are $$ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{clip}(Sg,c)/S &=g\min\!\left(1,\frac{c}{S\|g\|}\right),\\ \operatorname{clip}(g,c) &=g\min\!\left(1,\frac{c}{\|g\|}\right). \end{aligned} $$ Unscale first, then clip the complete accumulated gradient. The displayed numbers use the ideal norm formula; `clip_grad_norm_` adds a small denominator epsilon, so its floating-point result is approximately $(0.6,0.8)$. The API ordering follows [PyTorch's clipping example](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/notes/amp_examples.html#gradient-clipping); the pinned [implementation of `unscale_` and `step`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/5c4886908584029761b579af026dcfb627c84070/torch/amp/grad_scaler.py#L302-L480) also records the per-optimizer state that prevents a second automatic division. The source quotation is covered by the published [PyTorch license](/licenses/pytorch-v2.14.1-LICENSE.txt). ## Сколько памяти и времени можно сэкономить

changes.new: ### Rowwise and columnwise quantization retain different values ![[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/precision-2026-11/te-mxfp8-row-column.svg|MXFP8: блоки 1×32 по строкам и 32×1 по столбцам с отдельными масштабами]] *Figure 2. MXFP8 rowwise vs columnwise quantization layout. NVIDIA Transformer Engine documentation contributors, [original SVG](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TransformerEngine/blob/eb56ba22fd2b3c1fa4c962a4a575d4ba12d1fcbc/docs/features/low_precision_training/mxfp8/img/mxfp8_row_col.svg), [Apache-2.0](/licenses/nvidia-transformer-engine-Apache-2.0.txt). The complete 650×450 diagram, labels and geometry are retained. The unchanged upstream stylesheet is embedded for standalone display.* Each blue horizontal rectangle in the upper half is one group of 32 elements along a row. The lower half groups 32 elements along a column. Each orange scale belongs to its own group. Turning the stored array does not recalculate these scales from the original high-precision values. For a numerical example, fill a 32×32 matrix with ones and put $2^{20}$ at position $(0,0)$. Use E4M3 values and the smallest power-of-two restoration scale that keeps each group's maximum at or below 448. The row containing the outlier needs $s=4096$; every other row needs $s=2^{-8}$. Thus rowwise quantization loses the other 31 ones in row zero. Columnwise quantization instead loses the other 31 ones in column zero. These are different positions: | Position | Input | By row | By column | |---|---:|---:|---:| | $(0,0)$ | $2^{20}$ | $2^{20}$ | $2^{20}$ | | $(0,1)$ | 1 | 0 | 1 | | $(1,0)$ | 1 | 1 | 0 | | $(1,1)$ | 1 | 1 | 1 | The following CPU calculation casts normalized values to real E4M3FN, then restores FP32 values. Its scale arrays contain powers of two but are stored in FP32 for inspection. It does not construct a hardware-packed MXFP8 tensor, swizzle scales or launch a Blackwell GEMM. ~~~python import torch values = torch.ones((32, 32), dtype=torch.float32) values[0, 0] = 2**20 def rowwise_roundtrip(matrix): amax = matrix.abs().amax(dim=1, keepdim=True) scale = torch.pow(2.0, torch.ceil(torch.log2(amax / 448.0))) normalized = matrix / scale restored = normalized.to(torch.float8_e4m3fn).float() * scale return restored, scale rowwise, row_scale = rowwise_roundtrip(values) columnwise_t, column_scale = rowwise_roundtrip(values.T) columnwise = columnwise_t.T assert row_scale[0, 0].item() == 4096.0 assert row_scale[1, 0].item() == 2**-8 assert rowwise[0, 1].item() == 0.0 assert columnwise[0, 1].item() == 1.0 assert rowwise[1, 0].item() == 1.0 assert columnwise[1, 0].item() == 0.0 assert not torch.equal(rowwise.T, columnwise_t) print(int((rowwise == 0).sum()), int((columnwise == 0).sum())) # 31 31 ~~~ Here `rowwise_roundtrip` assumes nonzero finite groups. A general quantizer also needs policies for zero groups, nonfinite values and the available scale range. The example isolates the orientation error without those cases. Once the 31 small values have disappeared, a transpose cannot recover them. To prepare the other orientation, quantize the high-precision source again. This is the constraint in NVIDIA's [Handling transposes](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/transformer-engine/features/low_precision_training/mxfp8/mxfp8.html#handling-transposes); it does not mean every columnwise GEMM must physically transpose its inputs. ## Как проверить, что ускорение не испортило обучение

changes.old: `autocast` охватывает прямой проход и вычисление loss. Обратный проход выполняется вне этого контекста: он использует типы, выбранные соответствующими операциями прямого прохода. Перед ограничением нормы градиента вызывается `unscale_`, иначе порог ограничения будет применён к увеличенному в $S$ раз градиенту. `scaler.step` проверяет нечисловые значения и при необходимости пропускает шаг оптимизатора.
changes.new: `autocast` охватывает прямой проход и вычисление loss. Обратный проход выполняется вне этого контекста: он использует типы, выбранные соответствующими операциями прямого прохода. Перед ограничением нормы градиента вызывается `unscale_`, иначе порог ограничения будет применён к увеличенному в $S$ раз градиенту. `unscale_` также проверяет градиенты на `Inf` и `NaN`; `scaler.step` использует результат этой проверки и при необходимости пропускает обновление. После явного `unscale_` он не проверяет произвольно изменённые градиенты повторно.
